title: Genesis 29:1–14
context: After Bethel’s vow, Jacob journeys east and arrives at a well in Haran country. He meets Rachel, waters Laban’s flock, weeps, and is received into Laban’s house as bone and flesh—providence bringing the promised heir to the family from which Isaac’s wife had come.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: On Jacob at the well, Rachel, and Laban’s “bone and flesh”, a few classic voices from each tradition.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: She kept her father's sheep—She took the care of them, having servants under her that were employed about them when he understood that this was his kinswoman (probably he had heard of her name before) knowing what his errand was into that country, we may suppose it struck into his mind immediately, that this must be his wife, as one already smitten with an honest comely face (though it is likely, sun-burnt, and she in the homely dress of a shepherdess) he is wonderfully officious, and ready to serve her, ver.10, and addresses himself to her with tears of joy, and kisses of love, ver.11, she runs with all haste to tell her father, for she will by no means entertain her kinsman's address without her father's knowledge and approbation, ver.12.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 29:9)

reformed.quote: The great frankness of that age appears in this manner of meeting together; for, though the fraternal name is often abused by dishonest and wicked men, it is yet not to be doubted that friendly intercourse was then more faithfully cultivated than it is now. This was the reason why Jacob salutes unknown men as brethren, undoubtedly according to received custom.

verses.text: Then Jacob went on his journey, and came to the land of the children of the east.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jacob goes on, as he had vowed, into the east. The road is ordinary travel after an extraordinary night.

Listen here for a man who must still walk the promise. Grace met him at Bethel; now he responds by going where the LORD sent him.
verses.reformedNotes:
The journey continues under the God who stood at Bethel. East is not random; it is the appointed land of kin.

Reformed readers see providence in the route. The heir arrives where God already had a family waiting.

verses.text: He looked, and saw a well in the field, and saw three flocks of sheep lying there by it. For out of that well they watered the flocks. The stone on the well’s mouth was large.
verses.arminianNotes:
A well, flocks, a large stone—the scene of meeting is homely and blocked. Life waits on water someone must uncover.

God often places His people at ordinary wells. Grace does not skip the stone; it meets Jacob in the work of the field.
verses.reformedNotes:
Matthew’s servant found Rebekah at a well; Jacob finds the same kind of place. The large stone marks a barrier God will use.

The well is already there. Providence stocks the scene before Jacob speaks.

verses.text: There all the flocks were gathered. They rolled the stone from the well’s mouth, and watered the sheep, and put the stone back on the well’s mouth in its place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Custom rules the well: wait, roll, water, cover. Community protects the water and delays the thirsty.

Arminians note human order that is neither holy nor wicked in itself. Jacob will have to deal with neighbors, not a private miracle lane.
verses.reformedNotes:
The shepherds’ rhythm is settled. Stone on, stone off—local law at the well’s mouth.

God works inside custom. The delay will time Rachel’s arrival; the rule becomes the stage.

verses.text: Jacob said to them, “My relatives, where are you from?” They said, “We are from Haran.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He calls them brothers and asks origin. Haran is the name he needed—Rebekah’s country.

Honest questions find the place grace already named. Jacob uses courtesy and inquiry, not force, to locate kin.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Haran” is the word Isaac and Rebekah had sent him toward. The shepherds confirm the map.

God answers the first question with the right town. The covenant road has landed.

verses.text: He said to them, “Do you know Laban, the son of Nahor?” They said, “We know him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He names Laban, son of Nahor—family, not a stranger. They know him. The search narrows by relationship.

Arminians see responsible seeking. Jacob asks after the household God had already woven into Abraham’s line.
verses.reformedNotes:
Laban son of Nahor is the hinge of the errand. “We know him” is a small mercy with large history.

The God of Abraham still governs names. Kin is not luck; it is kept.

verses.text: He said to them, “Is it well with him?” They said, “It is well. See, Rachel, his daughter, is coming with the sheep.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Is it well?”—shalom for Laban—and they point: Rachel is coming with the sheep. Welcome arrives as a person on the path.

God’s timing arranges the meeting at the well. Jacob asked after welfare; God answers with the daughter who will shape the rest of the chapter.
verses.reformedNotes:
Shalom is reported, and Rachel is already in view. The narrative turns on “see.”

God brings the woman to the well while Jacob is still talking. Timing is the Lord’s.

verses.text: He said, “Behold, it is still the middle of the day, not time to gather the livestock together. Water the sheep, and go and feed them.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jacob urges work while the day is high—water and pasture, don’t idle. A traveler still speaks as a shepherd’s son.

The passage carries initiative. He does not wait passively; he presses the men toward the good they already know how to do.
verses.reformedNotes:
High day is no time to loaf at a closed well. Jacob’s counsel is practical and a little sharp.

Even the impatient word serves the scene. His energy will next move the stone God placed.

verses.text: They said, “We can’t, until all the flocks are gathered together, and they roll the stone from the well’s mouth. Then we will water the sheep.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They cannot—until all gather and the stone moves. Local duty binds them; Jacob’s hurry does not yet override it.

Constraints meet a willing man. Grace will not mock the shepherds’ “we can’t”; it will supply another pair of hands.
verses.reformedNotes:
“We can’t” is the rule of the well. The stone waits for the full company.

The delay is not wasted. It holds the moment until Rachel is close enough to see.

verses.text: While he was yet speaking with them, Rachel came with her father’s sheep, for she kept them.
verses.arminianNotes:
While he is still speaking, Rachel comes—shepherdess with her father’s sheep. The conversation is interrupted by the person it needed.

Classical Arminians rejoice in a timely arrival without erasing Rachel’s ordinary work. God uses a working woman, not a staged vision.
verses.reformedNotes:
Speech is still in the air when Rachel appears. Shepherdess is her calling, not a cameo.

Rachel arrives while Jacob is still speaking. The daughter of Laban enters on schedule the shepherds did not know they were keeping.

verses.text: When Jacob saw Rachel the daughter of Laban, his mother’s brother, and the sheep of Laban, his mother’s brother, Jacob went near, and rolled the stone from the well’s mouth, and watered the flock of Laban his mother’s brother.
verses.arminianNotes:
Kinship is named three times: Laban, mother’s brother, the flock. Jacob rolls the stone himself and waters the sheep. Love and duty move together.

For the hearer: grace-enabled strength serves another’s flock first. He does not wait for the group; he acts for family he has just recognized.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator drums “mother’s brother.” This is Rebekah’s house in the field. Jacob’s strength opens what custom had shut.

God supplies both the woman and the power to water her flock. The stone yields because the heir has arrived.

verses.text: Jacob kissed Rachel, and lifted up his voice, and wept.
verses.arminianNotes:
Kiss and loud weeping—relief, kinship, and hope without words. The well becomes a place of tears as well as water.

Classical Arminians honor the affection as human response to God’s kindness. Jacob is not a stoic; grace lets him feel the mercy of arrival.
verses.reformedNotes:
He weeps aloud. The man who fled Esau now stands among his mother’s people.

God brings the fugitive to family and unseals his grief. Tears here are theology—the promise has a human face.

verses.text: Jacob told Rachel that he was her father’s relative, and that he was Rebekah’s son. She ran and told her father.
verses.arminianNotes:
He identifies himself: kinsman, Rebekah’s son. Rachel runs with the news. Recognition spreads by a daughter’s feet.

Truth spoken plainly invites a household response. Jacob does not hide; he names the bond and lets Rachel act.
verses.reformedNotes:
Rebekah’s name opens the door. Rachel runs as her aunt’s story once ran from another well.

God repeats a family pattern. The same house that sent a bride west now receives the heir east.

verses.text: When Laban heard the news of Jacob, his sister’s son, he ran to meet Jacob, and embraced him, and kissed him, and brought him to his house. Jacob told Laban all these things.
verses.arminianNotes:
Laban runs, embraces, kisses, houses him. Jacob tells all these things—the road, the well, the vow’s background in the telling.

Arminian readers take the welcome as hospitality, later mixed with Laban’s craft. First gifts can be sincere even when later wages will sting.
verses.reformedNotes:
Laban’s haste mirrors his old run toward Abraham’s servant. House and kiss look like covenant kindness.

God uses even a calculating uncle to shelter Jacob. “All these things” now sit inside a household God chose as the next classroom.

verses.text: Laban said to him, “Surely you are my bone and my flesh.” Jacob stayed with him for a month.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Bone and my flesh” claims kinship; a month of staying tests it. Belonging is spoken before wages are named.

Family language is gift and risk. Jacob is truly kin; he must still watch how Laban will treat a kinsman’s labor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Bone and flesh is Genesis kinship-speech (2:23). A month’s stay is providence’s pause before the bargain.

God plants Jacob inside the household that will both bless and bruise him. The month is not delay outside the plan.
